title: Atlassian
summary: Problems whose patterns are commonly reported in Atlassian coding and code-design interviews, from Easy to Hard. Approximate and hand curated, not an official or verified question list.
lesson:
About this list
- Each problem practices a pattern that candidates commonly describe from Atlassian technical loops: stateful service and data-structure design, per-client rate limiting, ranked voting and leaderboards, file and collection aggregation, prefix and wildcard routing, grid simulations, intervals, and dependency ordering.
- Problems are grouped Easy, Medium, and Hard so you can start with focused warm-ups before practicing multi-operation code-design APIs and scaling edge cases.
- The selection is approximate. Interview formats vary across teams and levels, and interviewers choose their own prompts, so treat this track as pattern and code-craft practice rather than a prediction of what you will be asked.

What to expect
- Candidates often report practical, product-flavored rounds where clean class design, clear method contracts, and readable helper structure matter as much as asymptotic complexity.
- Prompts frequently begin with a simple single-tenant or single-window rule and add follow-ups such as multi-collection membership, wildcard route precedence, tie-breaking rules, or unused-quota credit carryover.
- Interviewers commonly probe how your code handles boundary timestamps, empty or overwritten entries, integer overflow on large counters or time gaps, and invalid arguments.
- You are usually expected to run or trace concrete test cases yourself and explain how you would make an in-memory component safe under concurrent access.

How to prepare
- Before coding, write down the exact invariants for ties, window boundaries, updates to existing keys, and whether rejected calls mutate state.
- Separate domain records from indexing structures so follow-up requirements can extend your class without rewriting every method.
- Test boundary transitions explicitly: exact cutoff timestamps, replacing an existing item, zero-count cleanup, and large 64-bit values.
- After passing the full check, practice explaining how you would add per-key locking, sharding, or bounded eviction if the component ran in production.
